summary: This proposed standard provides RSVP-TE extensions, including for GMPLS, to automatically collect Shared Risk Link Group information for the TE link formed by a Label Switched Path. SRLG information tells which links could fail together.

eli5.summary: Some roads cross the same bridge, so one flood closes them all. This lets a network path automatically report which risks it shares with others.

questions: how does rsvp-te collect srlg information
what is the srlg collection flag
why does dual homing need srlg information
subtitle: How an RSVP-TE signaled path can report which shared failure risks each of its links runs through.

tldr.problem: A label switched path used as a TE link needs to carry its Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) information, so others can tell which links could fail together, but that data was not collected automatically.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress node sets a new SRLG Collection Flag in the Attribute Flags TLV, and each hop adds a new SRLG subobject to the Route Record Object (RRO) in Path and Resv messages.
tldr.outcome: The endpoints learn the SRLGs of the whole LSP, for example to advertise it as a TE link or to build a diverse second path in a dual-homing setup.

today: RFC 8001 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Collect SRLG Information
sections.content:
A set of links forms a Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) if they share a resource whose failure can affect all of them. A hierarchical LSP or stitched LSP can be formed as a TE link and used to carry other LSPs, so it matters to know the SRLGs of the LSPs underneath.

This RFC provides a signaling mechanism that collects the SRLGs used by an LSP, which can then be advertised as properties of the TE link formed by that LSP. It extends RSVP-TE, including its GMPLS use.
sections.eli5: If two roads share one bridge, they can break together. The path learns which bridges it uses and tells the people who plan routes.

sections.title: The Dual-Homing Use Case
sections.content:
The RFC's example is a customer edge (CE) device connected to two provider edge (PE) devices. To get two end-to-end diverse LSPs, the second LSP must avoid the shared risks of the first, but SRLG information is normally not shared between the provider network and the client network. In the overlay model, routing information may not cross the User-Network Interface at all.

With this RFC, CE1 can retrieve the SRLGs of LSP1 when it is established, then pass them to PE2 in an EXCLUDE_ROUTE Object (XRO) or Explicit Exclusion Route Subobject (EXRS) in the setup request for LSP2. PE2 can then compute a path that is SRLG disjoint from LSP1. CE1 can also collect LSP2's SRLGs and re-signal LSP1 with SRLG exclusion, which keeps the two diverse when the provider restores failed connections.

Knowing SRLGs does not let a CE derive the provider topology, but an entity controlling several CE devices could learn some of it. For that reason PE devices are allowed to control how SRLGs are communicated outside the provider network.
sections.eli5: If you want two separate routes to grandma's house, you need to know the first route's bridges so the second route can skip them.

sections.title: The Three Stages and Their Requirements
sections.content:
Collection takes place in three stages: the ingress node requests it, nodes add SRLG data to the Path and Resv ROUTE_RECORD Objects (RROs) during signaling, and changes are sent later as updated Path and Resv messages.

The ingress node must be able to say whether SRLGs are to be collected, and nothing is collected without that explicit request. The request may be made so that every node must understand it, or so that the LSP is still set up if some nodes cannot supply SRLGs. The SRLG ID is a 32-bit quantity, as defined in RFC 4202.
sections.eli5: First the starter asks 'please write down your bridges', then everyone along the way writes theirs, and later they send corrections if something changes.

sections.title: The New Flag and Subobject
sections.content:
The request is a new SRLG Collection Flag in the Attribute Flags TLV (RFC 5420). A node MUST set it in an LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES object if collection is mandatory, or in an LSP_ATTRIBUTES object if collection is desired but not mandatory. It is meaningful on a Path message, and when set to 1 the SRLG information SHOULD be reported to the ingress and egress node.

The answer is a new RRO subobject, modeled on those in RFC 3209. It has a Type, an 8-bit Length (total octets including Type and Length), a 1-bit D-bit (not set means downstream, set means upstream), 15 reserved bits (SHOULD be zero on transmission, MUST be ignored on receipt), and then one 4-octet SRLG ID per collected SRLG.

A node MUST NOT push an SRLG subobject without also pushing an IPv4, IPv6, Unnumbered Interface ID or Path Key subobject. Because the RRO is managed as a stack, the SRLG subobject MUST be pushed before the node's IP address or link identifier, and within the hop it applies to. If a Confidential Path Segment is replaced by a Path Key Subobject per RFC 5553, its SRLG subobjects MAY be added again after the PKS.
sections.eli5: The request is a checkbox saying 'tell me your risks'. The reply is a list of numbered risk tags that each hop writes next to its own name, plus a mark for which direction they apply to.

sections.title: Signaling Procedures
sections.content:
A node MUST NOT add SRLG information unless the ingress asked for it in the Path message. If the request was in an LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES object and local policy says the SRLGs are not to be given to the endpoints, the node MUST reject the Path message with a PathErr carrying Error Code 2 (policy) and the subcode "SRLG Recording Rejected". If the request was in an LSP_ATTRIBUTES object, the Path message MUST NOT be rejected for that reason and is forwarded without SRLG subobjects.

If policy permits, the node SHOULD add its SRLG information to the RRO of the outgoing Path message and remember the request for Resv processing. If adding it would make the RRO too large, the SRLGs MUST NOT be added. For a mandatory request the RRO is dropped per RFC 3209, and for a non-mandatory request the node MAY omit some or all SRLGs. The egress node then starts an RRO in the Resv message, and the processing mirrors the Path direction until the ingress can extract the data.

An SRLG set for the upstream direction cannot be assumed to equal the downstream set. For a unidirectional LSP a node SHOULD include downstream SRLGs only. For a bidirectional LSP it SHOULD include both, in separate subobjects with the D-bit set correctly, upstream first, in the same order in Path and Resv. An SRLG ID that applies both ways SHOULD appear in both.

When the SRLGs of a link change, the refresh procedures in Section 4.4.3 of RFC 3209 MUST be used to tell affected LSPs, if local policy says the change be communicated.
sections.eli5: Nobody writes anything unless asked. If the request is 'must' and a hop does not want to share, it says no and the path is refused. If it is only 'please', the hop quietly skips it and the path still gets built.

sections.title: Domain Boundaries, Compatibility and Management
sections.content:
If local policy set by the network operator says so, a node MAY remove SRLG information from an RRO, and MAY add a summary or map the SRLGs to other values, though this SHOULD NOT be done unless policy mandates it. Border nodes of inter-domain or inter-layer networks MUST be configurable on whether they take part in collection and on whether SRLG IDs are exposed, summarized, mapped or removed.

A node that does not recognize the new flag follows RFC 5420: it passes the TLV on in an LSP_ATTRIBUTES object, or rejects the Path message if it is in an LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES object. A node that does not recognize the SRLG subobject ignores it and passes it on unchanged, per RFC 3209.

SRLG IDs SHOULD be unique. The procedures target layers and domains that belong to the same operator or to coordinated administrative groups, and ensuring coherence of IDs is out of scope, as are scenarios where coherence cannot be guaranteed.
sections.eli5: Border guards can hide or relabel the bridge numbers if the owner says so. Old equipment that does not understand the new request just passes it along.

sections.title: Security and IANA Assignments
sections.content:
The security discussion builds on RFC 3473 and the GMPLS security overview in RFC 5920. The procedures permit SRLG data to move between layers or domains during signaling, subject to local policy at the boundary, which the operator explicitly sets.

IANA assignments: bit 12 in the Attribute Flags registry for the SRLG Collection Flag, RRO subobject type 34 for the SRLG subobject, and Policy Control Failure subcode 21 for "SRLG Recording Rejected".
sections.eli5: Who may see the bridge numbers is up to the network owner. The new request, the new tag and the new 'no thanks' reply each got an official number.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Subobject type, 34 in the IANA registry.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length in octets, including Type and Length.

fields.name: D
fields.desc: Not set means downstream, set means upstream.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: SHOULD be zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt.

fields.name: SRLG ID 1 ... n
fields.desc: One 4-octet SRLG ID per collected SRLG; there can be several.

messages.note: Ingress asks for collection and adds its SRLGs to the RRO.

messages.label: Path + RRO with SRLGs
messages.note: Policy permitting, the node adds its own SRLG subobjects.

messages.label: Resv + RRO with SRLGs
messages.note: The egress starts the RRO in the Resv message.

messages.label: Resv + RRO with SRLGs
messages.note: The ingress can now extract the SRLG information.
